Optimization concepts

Source: vignettes/concepts.Rmd
concepts.Rmd
library(optcompR)

optcompR describes an optimization problem once, as variables, expressions, constraints and an objective, and then classifies it, chooses a capable solver This tutorial explains the distinctions that decide which solver applies and how to read its result, with a small model for each.

Convex and nonconvex

A problem is convex when it minimizes a convex function (or maximizes a concave one) over a convex set. Every local minimum of a convex problem is global. opt_classify() decides convexity for polynomial models of degree two and records how:

m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2)
opt_objective(m, x[1]^2 + x[1] * x[2] + x[2]^2)
cl <- opt_classify(m)
cl$convexity
#> [1] "convex"
cl$evidence
#> [1] "syntactic: objective is quadratic; constraint rows: none"                            
#> [2] "numerical eigenvalues: objective is convex (smallest eigenvalue 1 (tolerance 3e-09))"
opt_objective(m, x[1]^2 + 3 * x[1] * x[2] + x[2]^2)
opt_classify(m)$convexity
#> [1] "nonconvex"

For general nonlinear expressions convexity is reported as unknown; it is not guessed. Cone constraints are convex sets by construction, so a model whose only nonlinear structure is cones (with a linear or convex quadratic objective) is classified as convex "SOCP" or "CONIC"; see vignette("conic").

Continuous and mixed-integer

Integer variables make the feasible set a union of points or slices. The LP relaxation gives a bound, and branch and bound closes the gap:

m <- opt_model("max")
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", dim = 2, type = "integer", lower = 0)
opt_constraint(m, 2 * x[1] + 2 * x[2] <= 7)
opt_objective(m, x[1] + x[2])
r_int <- opt_solve(m)
opt_set_type(m, x, "continuous")
r_lp <- opt_solve(m)
c(integer = opt_objective_value(r_int), relaxation = opt_objective_value(r_lp))
#>    integer relaxation 
#>        3.0        3.5

Local and global optima 

m <- opt_model()
x <- opt_variable(m, "x", lower = -3, upper = 3, start = 2)
opt_objective(m, x^4 - 4 * x^2 + x)
r <- opt_solve(m, solver = "nloptr")
c(x = opt_value(r, x), f = opt_objective_value(r))
#>         x         f 
#>  1.346997 -2.618556
opt_status(r)
#> [1] "locally_optimal"
opt_set_start(m, x, -2)
r2 <- opt_solve(m, solver = "nloptr")
c(x = opt_value(r2, x), f = opt_objective_value(r2))
#>         x         f 
#> -1.472998 -5.444192

Different starts end in different local minima, and the status says locally_optimal, never optimal.

Feasible and optimal

A feasible point satisfies every constraint; an optimal point is feasible and has the best objective. Solvers stopped by limits may return a feasible point that is not proven optimal; opt_has_solution(), opt_status() and opt_gap() together tell which case applies.

Primal and dual

The primal variables are the decisions x. The dual variables y price the constraints: y_i = \partial f^* / \partial b_i. In optcompR this sign convention holds for both minimization and maximization, and opt_check() verifies the KKT stationarity condition \nabla f(x) - J(x)^\top y - z = 0.

Termination and solution status

opt_status() reports why the solver stopped (optimal, infeasible, time_limit, …). opt_primal_status() and opt_dual_status() report whether the returned vectors are feasible. A time_limit termination with a feasible_point primal status is a usable incumbent.

Derivatives and sensitivity of optima

The gradient of the objective, \nabla f(x), describes the model function. The sensitivity of the optimum, \partial f^* / \partial b, describes the optimization problem as a whole; by the envelope theorem it equals the dual. See vignette("sensitivity"). The derivative of the optimal point itself, \partial x^* / \partial p, follows from differentiating the KKT conditions and is computed by opt_solution_jacobian(); see vignette("solution-derivatives").
